newsitem.title: DENMARK: Aid bodies review Europe hit by poverty, violence.
newsitem.headline: Aid bodies review Europe hit by poverty, violence.

text.p: Representatives of 52 European Red Cross and Red Crescent groups meet next week to assess future humanitarian activity in a continent threatened by mounting poverty, conflict, ethnic tension, urban violence and health problems in the post-Cold War era.

"We tend to focus all the time on the European Union and forget that there is another Europe which lives in a completely different world," Joergen Poulsen, secretary-general of Danish Red Cross, told Reuters on Friday.

"This other Europe has suffered a major breakdown since the collapse of the Iron Curtain. Over 50 million people in Russia and another 40 million in former Soviet bloc countries are living below the poverty line," he said. "We have a huge task ahead of us in holding these societies together. We want to offer them a partnership," Poulsen said. A conference, to held in Copenhagen from March 17-20, brings together the international Red Cross and the Moslem Red Crescent organisations at national and international level, governmental and non-governmental as well as voluntary organisations and United Nations observers.
The Danish Red Cross is hosting the meeting along with national societies in the rest of the Nordic region, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland,
"This is the first time Red Cross and Crescent societies from both sides of the old ideological divide in Europe meet since communism fell. We must learn to collaborate and cooperate," Poulsen said.
"I am optimistic that we can weld eastern and western Europe together through an active humanitarian partnership in the fight against poverty," he said.

The post-communist period in eastern Europe has seen vast changes with war, growing ethnic tension, social polarisation, youth drug abuse, violence and new health and environmental problems aggravated by decreasing public resources placing an ever escalating responsibility on humanitarian organisations.

"Abject poverty reigns in former Soviet countries, people are dying of starvation, the lifespan is falling, child deaths are more frequent than ever before, old illnesses we thought were eradicated are spreading there," he said.
"It would be terribly dangerous not to help these countries overcome their catastrophic problems, we must help them to function better, to enable them to become democratic," Poulsen said.
